question: What is Inner Monologue in Moshi and why is it used?
answer: Inner Monologue is a training and inference procedure in Moshi that jointly models text and audio tokens, allowing the model to fully exploit the knowledge imparted from the text modality while remaining a speech‑to‑speech system. [1][2] It decomposes speech into a chain of text, semantic and acoustic tokens and predicts this structured sequence in a hierarchical manner, enabling the model to represent all utterances as both text and speech rather than switching between modalities. [1] Because the acoustic tokens are integrated into the same generative model, Moshi can generate arbitrary voices and conditions instead of being limited to a single speaker. [1] The hierarchical modeling allows decomposing the generation task without increasing the sequence length of the Transformer outputs, and the per‑frame decomposition means each prediction step outputs a speech frame, making Moshi compatible with real‑time generation. [1] Finally, when combined with a delay between token types, Inner Monologue enables deriving streaming TTS and ASR systems from Moshi, supporting full‑duplex spoken dialogue. [1]
sources: [1] Moshi (arXiv 2410.00037v1), §2 Related Work, pp.5-6 | [2] Moshi (arXiv 2410.00037v1), §3.1 Overview, pp.6-7
key_facts: predicts time-aligned text tokens before (as a prefix to) audio tokens ; improves factuality and linguistic quality of generated speech

question: What does the smoothing module in H-Net's dynamic chunking do?
answer: The smoothing module transforms the discrete chunking operation into a continuous, differentiable one by applying an exponential moving average (EMA) that blends the current compressed representation with the previous one weighted by the boundary confidence score [𝑃𝑡] [1]. This allows gradients to flow through chunk boundaries during training without stochastic exploration, preserving autoregressive causality because each smoothed output depends only on past compressed representations [2]. When the boundary confidence is high (𝑃𝑡 ≈ 1.0) the EMA preserves the discrete boundary (¯𝑧𝑡 ≈ 𝑧𝑡), whereas low‑confidence boundaries (𝑃𝑡 ≈ 0.5) are smoothed with information from earlier chunks, providing an adaptive error‑correction mechanism [1]. By smoothly interpolating between discrete choices based on confidence, the module also stabilizes training and prevents overfitting to suboptimal chunking patterns early in training [1].
sources: [1] H-Net (arXiv 2507.07955v2), §2.2.2 Dechunking, pp.6-7 | [2] H-Net (arXiv 2507.07955v2), §2.4 Autoregressive Training and Inference, pp.9-10
key_facts: interpolates representations using the router's outputs ; attenuates the effect of uncertain boundaries, improving learnability
